beats.text: Git was right, and the engineer deleted a branch with one commit that existed nowhere else under a name. The rule behind -d isn't about main. It's about the upstream, the branch your branch is set up to follow. Without the rule, you'll read a correct warning as a bug, and override it. Almost everyone does, once. This video gives you the rule, and every git branch and git switch operation with its risk label. Keep that refusal in mind. It comes back.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. A commit is one saved snapshot of your project. A branch is a ref: a name that points at one commit. HEAD is Git's note of which branch you're on. This video is the working vocabulary on top of those facts.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. A commit is one saved snapshot of your project. A branch is a ref: a name that points at one commit. HEAD is Git's note of which branch you're on. This video is the working vocabulary on top of those facts.

beats.text: Two commands today. git branch lists refs under refs/heads/, creates one at a commit, deletes one, renames one, or moves one. It never touches the working tree, the files you see and edit. git switch changes which branch HEAD names, and updates the working tree and the index, Git's list of what goes into the next commit. For each operation I'll say what moves and how risky it is, and for the red one I'll answer the five questions first.

It never touches the working tree, the files you see and edit. `git switch` changes which branch HEAD names, and updates the working tree and the index, Git's list of what goes into the next commit. For each operation I'll say what moves and how risky it is, and for the red one I'll answer the five questions first.

beats.text: Listing. git branch lists local branches. -v adds the tip, meaning the commit the branch points at, and its title. For branches with an upstream, it adds how far they are ahead or behind it. -vv names the upstream. -r lists refs/remotes/, the remote-tracking branches, your record of the branches on the remote, the server copy. -a lists both namespaces.
beats.tele: Listing. `git branch` lists local branches. `-v` adds the tip, meaning the commit the branch points at, and its title. For branches with an upstream, it adds how far they are ahead or behind it. `-vv` names the upstream. `-r` lists `refs/remotes/`, the remote-tracking branches, your record of the branches on the remote, the server copy. `-a` lists both namespaces.

beats.text: Merged, not merged, contains. --merged lists "branches whose tips are reachable from" the named commit, HEAD by default. Reachable means you get there by walking from commit to parent. In this part of the lab repository, main walks back to docs/metrics and feature/f1, so they're merged. --no-merged lists the others. --contains <commit> turns the question around: which branches reach this commit?
beats.tele: Merged, not merged, contains. `--merged` lists "branches whose tips are reachable from" the named commit, HEAD by default. Reachable means you get there by walking from commit to parent. In this part of the lab repository, `main` walks back to `docs/metrics` and `feature/f1`, so they're merged. `--no-merged` lists the others. `--contains <commit>` turns the question around: which branches reach this commit?

beats.text: Deleting. git branch -d is 🟡 CAUTION: it deletes the ref after checking merge status. git branch -D is 🔴 DANGEROUS: it deletes regardless. Both delete the branch's reflog with it. The reflog is a local journal of where that name has pointed.
beats.tele: Deleting. `git branch -d` is 🟡 CAUTION: it deletes the ref after checking merge status. `git branch -D` is 🔴 DANGEROUS: it deletes regardless. Both delete the branch's reflog with it. The reflog is a local journal of where that name has pointed.

beats.text: What does it change? It deletes the ref and its reflog, with no merge check. What can it destroy? The branch reflog, and the only name of commits that were never checked out. How do you preview? git log --oneline main..<branch> lists the commits that only this branch reaches.
beats.tele: What does it change? It deletes the ref and its reflog, with no merge check. What can it destroy? The branch reflog, and the only name of commits that were never checked out. How do you preview? `git log --oneline main..<branch>` lists the commits that only this branch reaches.

beats.text: How do you recover? git branch <name> <id>, while the objects exist. The ID is in the deletion message, after the word "was", and the HEAD reflog still lists the commit if it was ever checked out. When is it appropriate? For a branch whose commits you've decided to abandon, or that you know to be squash-merged.
beats.tele: How do you recover? `git branch <name> <id>`, while the objects exist. The ID is in the deletion message, after the word "was", and the HEAD reflog still lists the commit if it was ever checked out. When is it appropriate? For a branch whose commits you've decided to abandon, or that you know to be squash-merged.

beats.text: The -d rule. The manual: "The branch must be fully merged in its upstream branch, or in HEAD if no upstream was set". So the rule is about the upstream, not about main. That gives two cases that surprise people. fix/typo-readme isn't merged into HEAD, but it's pushed and equal to its upstream, the dashed label. -d deletes it, with a warning. And feature/f1 is merged into HEAD, but it has one commit that its upstream lacks. -d refuses. Read both messages before reaching for -D.
beats.tele: The `-d` rule. The manual: "The branch must be fully merged in its upstream branch, or in HEAD if no upstream was set". So the rule is about the upstream, not about `main`. That gives two cases that surprise people. `fix/typo-readme` isn't merged into HEAD, but it's pushed and equal to its upstream, the dashed label. `-d` deletes it, with a warning. And `feature/f1` is merged into HEAD, but it has one commit that its upstream lacks. `-d` refuses. Read both messages before reaching for `-D`.

beats.text: Renaming and forcing. git branch -m is 🟡 CAUTION: it renames the ref, its reflog and its configuration section in one step, and logs the rename. The upstream still points at the old name on the remote, because renaming a local branch changes nothing on the remote.
beats.tele: Renaming and forcing. `git branch -m` is 🟡 CAUTION: it renames the ref, its reflog and its configuration section in one step, and logs the rename. The upstream still points at the old name on the remote, because renaming a local branch changes nothing on the remote.

beats.text: git branch -f is 🟡 CAUTION too. Without -f, git branch refuses to change an existing branch. With it, the ref moves, and the reflog records the reset, so the old position is one entry away. A branch that is checked out in a worktree can't be force-moved at all. git reset is the command for that.
beats.tele: `git branch -f` is 🟡 CAUTION too. Without `-f`, `git branch` refuses to change an existing branch. With it, the ref moves, and the reflog records the reset, so the old position is one entry away. A branch that is checked out in a worktree can't be force-moved at all. `git reset` is the command for that.

beats.text: git switch. In one sentence: git switch changes which branch HEAD names, and updates the index and the working tree to that branch's commit, refusing when a local change would be lost. It is 🟢 SAFE.
beats.tele: `git switch`. In one sentence: `git switch` changes which branch HEAD names, and updates the index and the working tree to that branch's commit, refusing when a local change would be lost. It is 🟢 SAFE.

beats.text: git switch <branch> points HEAD at the branch, then makes the index and working tree match its tip. -c <new> creates the branch first. The manual calls it "the transactional equivalent" of git branch followed by git switch. -C resets an existing branch like git branch -f, and is 🟡 CAUTION.
beats.tele: `git switch <branch>` points HEAD at the branch, then makes the index and working tree match its tip. `-c <new>` creates the branch first. The manual calls it "the transactional equivalent" of `git branch` followed by `git switch`. `-C` resets an existing branch like `git branch -f`, and is 🟡 CAUTION.

beats.text: Three more. --detach points HEAD at a commit instead of a branch. - means @{-1}, the previously checked-out branch or commit. And --orphan <new> creates an unborn branch, one with no commit yet, and removes all tracked files from the working tree. So the next commit starts a disconnected history.
beats.tele: Three more. `--detach` points HEAD at a commit instead of a branch. `-` means `@{-1}`, the previously checked-out branch or commit. And `--orphan <new>` creates an unborn branch, one with no commit yet, and removes all tracked files from the working tree. So the next commit starts a disconnected history.

beats.text: Local changes. Switching doesn't require a clean working tree. An edit you haven't staged or committed exists only in the working tree. A change in a file that is identical on both branches is carried along. A change in a file that differs is refused. Then you commit, stash, or use --merge.
beats.tele: Local changes. Switching doesn't require a clean working tree. An edit you haven't staged or committed exists only in the working tree. A change in a file that is identical on both branches is carried along. A change in a file that differs is refused. Then you commit, stash, or use `--merge`.

beats.text: A version note from the textbook on that last option. Since Git 2.55, git switch -m saves the local changes in a stash, a shelf for uncommitted work, and reapplies them. The recommendation is to commit or stash yourself, and to use --merge when you understand the stash it may leave behind.
beats.tele: A version note from the textbook on that last option. Since Git 2.55, `git switch -m` saves the local changes in a stash, a shelf for uncommitted work, and reapplies them. The recommendation is to commit or stash yourself, and to use `--merge` when you understand the stash it may leave behind.

beats.text: git checkout. It does the same jobs with older spellings. Learn them to read other people's scripts, and write switch and restore yourself. git checkout <name> guesses whether you mean a branch or a path, and that's the ambiguity the two newer commands remove. One difference in behavior: switch --orphan empties the working tree, while checkout --orphan keeps the files and stages them.
beats.tele: `git checkout`. It does the same jobs with older spellings. Learn them to read other people's scripts, and write `switch` and `restore` yourself. `git checkout <name>` guesses whether you mean a branch or a path, and that's the ambiguity the two newer commands remove. One difference in behavior: `switch --orphan` empties the working tree, while `checkout --orphan` keeps the files and stages them.

beats.text: The version note. git switch and git restore exist since Git 2.23, and are no longer labelled experimental from Git 2.51. git checkout still does all of the jobs and is not scheduled for removal.

beats.text: The one red switch. git switch --discard-changes, also -f, is 🔴 DANGEROUS. It changes the index and working tree to the target, and destroys uncommitted edits in the files it touches. There's no preview beyond git status, and no recovery for content that was never staged. It's appropriate only when you've decided to throw the edits away. Twig looks worried, fairly. It is not run in this video.

beats.text: Quick quiz. Which of these can change files in your working tree? A, git branch -f. B, git branch -m. Or C, git switch. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. Which of these can change files in your working tree? A, `git branch -f`. B, `git branch -m`. Or C, `git switch`. Your answer?

beats.text: C, and only C. git branch only moves names. It never touches the working tree. Its risk is that a name was the only way to find some commits.

beats.text: git switch moves HEAD and changes files. Its design is to refuse whenever changing a file would lose an edit, and that's why it is green.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Overriding a -d refusal with -D without reading the message. Root cause: -d tests the branch against its upstream, or against HEAD when it has no upstream; the message says which test failed.
beats.tele: Overriding a `-d` refusal with `-D` without reading the message. Root cause: `-d` tests the branch against its upstream, or against HEAD when it has no upstream; the message says which test failed.

beats.text: Believing that -d protects everything unmerged. Root cause: a branch that equals its upstream is deleted with a warning, even if HEAD does not contain it.
beats.tele: Believing that `-d` protects everything unmerged. Root cause: a branch that equals its upstream is deleted with a warning, even if HEAD does not contain it.

beats.text: Expecting git branch -m to rename the branch on the server. Root cause: renaming a local branch changes nothing on the remote; the upstream configuration still names the old branch.
beats.tele: Expecting `git branch -m` to rename the branch on the server. Root cause: renaming a local branch changes nothing on the remote; the upstream configuration still names the old branch.

beats.text: git branch -f main <x> fails with "used by worktree". Root cause: a checked-out branch cannot be force-moved; that is what git reset is for.
beats.tele: `git branch -f main <x>` fails with "used by worktree". Root cause: a checked-out branch cannot be force-moved; that is what `git reset` is for.

beats.text: git switch refuses: local changes would be overwritten. Root cause: the edited file differs between the two branch tips; commit or stash first.
beats.tele: `git switch` refuses: local changes would be overwritten. Root cause: the edited file differs between the two branch tips; commit or stash first.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. A backend team's cleanup script loops over local branches. It runs git branch -D on every branch that git branch --merged main lists, plus, for good measure, every branch older than a month. One engineer loses a spike that was never pushed, and never checked out on that machine again: no upstream, no HEAD reflog entry near the top, and the branch reflog deleted with the branch.

beats.text: The safer script uses -d, lets Git apply its rule, prints every refusal, and leaves the refused branches to a human, who previews each with git log --oneline main..<branch>.

beats.text: Let's land this. You should now be able to say: git branch only moves names and never touches the working tree. Creating a branch is green. Renaming, force-moving and -d are amber. -D is red, because it deletes the ref and its reflog with no merge check. -d requires the branch to be fully merged in its upstream, or in HEAD if it has none.
